newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Issues at the European security summit in Lisbon.
newsitem.headline: Issues at the European security summit in Lisbon.

text.p: Keeping peace and stability in Europe tops the agenda when leaders from the 54-nation Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) meet for a summit in Lisbon on Monday and Tuesday.
The organisation, which holds summits every two years, groups the United States and Canada with all European nations, although Yugoslavia has been suspended since 1992.
U.S. President Bill Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin are not attending, but will be represented by Vice President Al Gore and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin respectively.
Following are the main agenda items for Lisbon:
RUSSIA AND NATO ENLARGEMENT

Russia wants to strengthen the OSCE and give it more authority, to counterbalance NATO's growing influence in European security. Moscow opposes the Western alliance's plans to take on new members from Central and Eastern Europe. There is, however, little support for Russia's proposals at the summit and diplomats say there could be disagreements.
FORMER YUGOSLAVIA

The OSCE has taken a major role in implementing the Bosnian peace agreement, organising September's elections, overseeing an arms control agreement for former Yugoslavia and monitoring human rights and democratic freedoms in the region.
The summit is expected to approve a detailed role for the OSCE over the next two years, working in parallel with the NATO-led peace force in Bosnia. Bosnia and Croatia will attend the meeting.
BELARUS, CHECHNYA, NAGORNO-KARABAKH

The crisis in Belarus is expected to be discussed, particularly since hardline President Alexander Lukashenko has said he will come to Lisbon. Western countries have criticised his efforts to extend presidential powers.
The OSCE helped broker an end to the conflict in the breakaway region of Chechnya and will discuss possible involvement in monitoring local elections due there in January.

The Budapest summit of 1994 agreed to send a peacekeeping force to the troubled enclave of Nagorno-Karabakh in Azerbaijan, if a proper peace settlement could be reached to cement a ceasefire there. This has so far failed to happen, with talks in Helsinki last week making little progress, and diplomats say plans for the peacekeeping force are now on ice.
ARMS CONTROL

Following the end of the Cold War, the OSCE has taken on responsibilities in the field of arms control throughout Europe. The summit will discuss how to extend and adapt a landmark deal on cutting military hardware, signed between NATO and the now-defunct Warsaw Pact in 1990, so that it reflects the changed security situation on the continent.
DOCUMENTS AND DECLARATIONS
The summit will adopt a declaration entitled "Our Common Security", outlining how all can work together in the 21st century and put the era of confrontation firmly behind them.

It will promise continued work on a "security model", which member states have been struggling to define for two years, to ensure that all countries and organisations such as NATO and the European Union work smoothly together.
Diplomats say the document will be short on concrete details because of differences among the member states on issues such as NATO enlargement.
Switzerland holds the chairmanship of the OSCE this year, followed by Denmark in 1997. The summit will formally approve Poland to take over the job in 1998.
